summary.text: The periodic table arranges the chemical elements into rows called periods and columns called groups.
Elements are listed in order of increasing atomic number, and elements in the same group tend to show similar chemical characteristics.
Because of that pattern, it is relatively easy to predict the chemical properties of an element if you know the properties of the elements around it.

items.prompt: Oxygen, sulfur and selenium share one column of the table. What puts them there?

options.label: They each have four electrons in the outer p-subshell
They have almost identical atomic masses
They have exactly the same number of protons
They were all discovered in the same year

items.explain: Columns are set by electron configuration: elements with the same number of electrons in a subshell share a column.

items.prompt: Two atoms each have six protons, but one has seven neutrons and the other has six. Where do they go in the table?

options.label: Different elements, so they sit in separate boxes
One shared spot, because they are the same element
Different groups, because their weights differ
A separate row for the heavier one

items.explain: Atoms with the same number of protons but different neutrons are isotopes of one element, and they are always grouped under a single element.

items.prompt: A student wants to guess how an unfamiliar element will behave. What is the best shortcut the table offers?

options.label: Look up when it was first discovered
Weigh a single atom of it
Compare it with the elements around it
Check which language its name came from

items.explain: Elements with similar chemical properties generally fall in the same group, so the neighbours predict its behaviour.

items.prompt: Americium and everything heavier up to oganesson cannot be dug up anywhere on Earth. How do people get them?

options.label: Separating them from ordinary air
Mining rare ores deep underground
Boiling large amounts of seawater
Making them artificially in a lab

items.explain: Elements 95 to 118 occur only when synthesized in laboratories.

items.prompt: Mendeleev's 1869 table had blank spots because some elements were still undiscovered. How did he use them?

options.label: He treated them as errors and removed those rows
He predicted some properties of the absent elements
He filled them with elements picked at random
He used them to define atomic numbers

items.explain: He used the periodic law to predict some properties of some of the missing elements.

items.prompt: Atoms of one element can carry different numbers of neutrons, yet the listed atomic weight is a steady figure. Why?

options.label: Neutrons are stripped out whenever the element is purified
Only the lightest form is ever counted in the table
Each form turns up in a steady share, so it is an average
Neutrons add no weight, so every atom matches exactly

items.explain: Each isotope usually occurs with a characteristic abundance, so the atomic weight is the average mass of a naturally occurring atom. Neutrons do affect weight.

paragraphs.heading: A grid of the elements
paragraphs.text: The periodic table sorts the chemical elements into rows, called periods, and columns, called groups. An element is a class of atom picked out by its atomic number, which is the count of protons in the nucleus. The table lists the elements by rising atomic number. Hydrogen is number 1, helium is 2 and lithium is 3, and each has a short symbol: H, He and Li.

paragraphs.heading: Why the pattern repeats
paragraphs.text: The layout is a picture of the periodic law: line the elements up by atomic number and their properties roughly come round again. A new row starts when a new electron shell gets its first electron. Columns depend on how an atom's electrons are arranged. Oxygen, sulfur and selenium share a column because each has four electrons in its outermost p-subshell. Members of one group tend to behave alike chemically, so knowing an element's neighbours makes it fairly easy to guess how it will behave.

paragraphs.heading: Trends across the grid
paragraphs.text: Besides rows and columns, the table is split into four roughly rectangular regions called blocks. Patterns run up and down it, across it and even along its diagonals. Metallic character grows as you move down a group, or leftward along a period. Nonmetallic character grows the opposite way, from the bottom left corner toward the top right.

paragraphs.heading: Mendeleev and the gaps
paragraphs.text: The first table that chemists broadly accepted came from the Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev in 1869. He tied the chemical properties of elements to their atomic mass. Not every element was known yet, so his table had empty spaces, and he used the periodic law to forecast some properties of some of the missing ones. Early in the 20th century, the discovery of atomic numbers and pioneering quantum mechanics explained the law by shedding light on the inside of the atom.

paragraphs.heading: Isotopes share one box
paragraphs.text: Neutrons change how much an atom weighs but not which element it is. Atoms that share a proton count but differ in neutrons are called isotopes of one element. Carbon, for instance, always has six protons; most carbon atoms have six neutrons, about one per cent have seven, and a very small fraction have eight. The table never splits isotopes apart. The atomic mass it shows is usually a weighted average of the isotopes found in nature.

paragraphs.heading: How far the table reaches
paragraphs.text: Today 118 elements are known. The first 94 occur naturally on Earth, while the other 24, from americium to oganesson, appear only when made in laboratories. Together the 118 fill the first seven rows, though the heaviest still need chemical testing to confirm they belong where they sit. New discoveries will add rows beyond the seventh, and calculations suggest that unknown region may not follow the familiar patterns.
